title: Anyone using AI to teach themselves how to build a game rather than have it build the game?
author: SuspiciouslyJoyous
selftext: As title says. I’m a middle-aged English teacher so absolutely brand new to this kind of thing but I’ve always been a gamer and I’ve always wanted to write stories. Have had a story in my head for years that I wanted to tell and recently decided that I’d make it a game rather than a book. Now I’m using AI to teach myself how to build a game rather than have it it do for me. A few months ago I didn’t even know what Godot was and, so far, it’s such a satisfying process! I have very quickly realised that to make this game look how like the vision I have in my head, this is gonna be a hell of a longer process than I planned for (I had a 6 month plan ha ha ha ha).

comments.author: ongix
comments.body: I think a bit of both. Where I feel AI needs less supervision or rather I can validate easily I let it loose. And where I want to set the tone or I need that fine detail I let it teach me the specifics which is really satisfying as you said.

replies.author: SuspiciouslyJoyous
replies.body:
Is developing games something you’ve done previously or decided to give it a go with the help of AI only? 

I feel like because I have the  whole thing mapped out so precisely, I’m so cautious with every letter of the script but I’d have never got past the first line without the guidance of AI.

replies.author: asprincontainer
replies.body: Not sure what platform you’re using. But if you’re using Claude, you should try uploading your whole mapped out idea to the Claude.md file. If you actually have a solid plan with rules and a solid vision, it follows it pretty damn well.

replies.author: SuspiciouslyJoyous
replies.body: Appreciate it! I’m using ChatGPT and I did give it a pretty detailed map (planned on Milanote as, like I say, it’s very very narrative/story-based) but I don’t want it to do all the programming for me, I want it to give me the skills to eventually be able to do that without its input at all. Maybe Claude is a better option but ChatGPT often gets very basic things wrong like established font/hex codes etc hence my very very cautious use.

comments.author: ZymzAlchemy
comments.body:
It depends on yoiur goal. Are you trying to one off projects for yourself at home, or learn to build products you can share, and do you plan to commercialize? 

As someone with decades of experience with this stuff, I would suggest gathering some useful materials to teach yourself 'how to build a game' an then maybe use the AI to help you better understand and explore the concepts. 

It is my opinion (and YMMV), that AI is currently not mature enough to perform the architecture and construction of an entire functional project from the ground up without experienced human intervention. These are my findings over and over. 

Having said that, it can be useful for exploring concepts and rapid drafting, but if your core goal is to 'become a game designer/developer' then AI alone cannot teach you the skills you need to do this well.

TLDR - Do the manual work, learn the right skills, use AI as a rapid exploration and development assistant, do not trust it's output without learning how to verify it's accuracy, in this process you will learn.  

Be well, and keep creating.

replies.author: SuspiciouslyJoyous
replies.body:
This is super helpful and I appreciate all the advice from an experienced hand! 

And that’s the route I’m heading down, I’ve used AI to explain how I do each step etc but I’m then doing a little extra research (on here, YouTube etc) to find out why and what it’s for so that I’m actually learning as I go. 

I guess the end goal is to have a game to release but it’s going to be a long road and I’m just kind of enjoying learning about a completely different world for now.

replies.author: ZymzAlchemy
replies.body:
The best advice I can give to you is document everything. Save everything. Even things you think are trash, some day you might find something useful in there. 

Write a roadmap before you start a project, this outlines what you want. Every mechanic, every level, every detail as you see it. Then use this to build a blueprint. Keep the build phases small and isolated to specific tasks to prevent your agent from drifting. Use GIT because you will run into trouble and it will help you unravel it.

replies.author: SuspiciouslyJoyous
replies.body: Thank you so much! And absolutely! I have every minute detail saved in various places and make a backup everytime I finish working on something each day. I really do appreciate the advice.

comments.author: jopazo
comments.body:
Yeah, me and a friend... We use it to teach ourselves, we make the game to learn X thing then dump it bc honestly they are just practice stuff (they suck as games).

We will try to make a real game soon :3

comments.author: Still_Explorer
comments.body:
Typically when I would start something new that I would be unfamiliar and inexperienced in, I would seek project references on GitHub.

Having some reference as a foundation is like having some ground truth and will allow you to remain steady and sure about where you're going and what you're doing.

If for example you start getting seconds thoughts and questioning things more than needed, then the project reference can clear things up by showing you what worked before for someone and by great percentage would work the same for you.

Though it makes sense that you will use some parts from reference but also improvise other parts, so is not that you would be constantly sticking to what already exists. However the idea is that once about the 60% to 70% is well established and known, only the rest few parts would be unknown and you would have to improvise there.

This makes things more predictable and organized, rather that you would normally go 100% by random chance.

replies.author: SuspiciouslyJoyous
replies.body:
Thanks so much for this, I’ll 100% add this to my resource list and have a read through as I’ve not heard of GitHub. 

And I absolutely work best when my work is organised and predictable and that helps me learn.

replies.author: SuspiciouslyJoyous

comments.author: No_Training_9980
comments.body: Im working on a tower defense roguelite game (my first game ever) and i am always asking the AI how and why it did something so i can really learn how everything works.

replies.author: SuspiciouslyJoyous
replies.body: Yes! It’s the “why?” that really helps!

comments.author: Livid_Shallot5701
comments.body: No. It's 1000x times faster than I would be. 2 weeks ago it build physics, water physics, biome generators and asset generators in a single day. I would have taken at least a year even with all the information help possible if I would not copy paste code

comments.author: craigitsfriday
comments.body: Hey OP, I've actually had some success doing this exact thing. Ive been a unity dev for 16 years and wanted to learn blueprints in Unreal. Using Claude Code I've prompted a helpful tutor that walks me through blueprint creation using the MCP connection. Being an educator, you may also get some use from GAIL's prompt library. It may give you some ideas on creating your prompt. https://gail.wharton.upenn.edu/prompt-library/

replies.author: SuspiciouslyJoyous
replies.body: This is awesome, thanks so much, I’ll save this as a resource. Great to hear someone else is doing the same as me!

comments.author: Disastrous-Round-150
comments.body: If you really want to learn to build games you should do it from scratch without using any game engines.

replies.author: Left-Excitement3829
replies.body: Do u use a Babbage machine. And semaphore ?

replies.author: SuspiciouslyJoyous
replies.body: Interesting. What do you mean by this?

replies.author: Disastrous-Round-150
replies.body: The way games were made before game engines, just using a programming language like c++ and glsl (shader language) and lay out all the basics you want in the game and get the AI to break down each step it does.

comments.author: StellarSoupStudio
comments.body: That's great! I encourage you to also learn some stuff about more generalized development topics mainly the software git which is a version control tool, and places to store your versions like Github and Gitlab and others. Implementing things like this now is not obvious for new developers but make projects a lot easier to fix years on, and a lot easier to deploy in the future.
